{{Short description|On repetitions in infinite strings of symbols}}
'''Dejean's theorem''' (formerly '''Dejean's conjecture''') is a statement about repetitions in infinite [[String (computer science)|strings of symbols]]. It belongs to the field of [[combinatorics on words]]; it was conjectured in 1972 by Françoise Dejean and proven in 2009 by Currie and Rampersad and, independently, by Rao.{{r|rs}}

==Context==
In the study of strings, [[concatenation]] is seen as analogous to multiplication of numbers. For instance, if <math>s</math> is any string,
then the concatenation <math>ss</math> of two copies of <math>s</math> is called the square of <math>s</math>, and denoted <math>s^2</math>. This exponential notation may also be extended to fractional powers: if <math>s</math> has length <math>\ell</math>, and <math>e</math> is a non-negative [[rational number]] of the form <math>n/\ell</math>, then <math>s^e</math> denotes the string formed by the first <math>n</math> characters of the infinite repetition <math>sssss\dots</math>.{{r|rs}}

A [[square-free word]] is a string that does not contain any square as a substring. In particular, it avoids repeating the same symbol consecutively, repeating the same pair of symbols, etc. [[Axel Thue]] showed that there exists an infinite square-free word using a three-symbol alphabet, the sequence of differences between consecutive elements of the [[Thue–Morse sequence]]. However, it is not possible for an infinite two-symbol word (or even a two-symbol word of length greater than three) to be square-free.{{r|rs}}

For alphabets of two symbols, however, there do exist infinite cube-free words,
words with no substring of the form <math>sss</math>. One such example is the [[Thue–Morse sequence]] itself; another is the [[Kolakoski sequence]]. More strongly, the Thue–Morse sequence contains no substring that is a power strictly greater than two.{{r|rs}}

In 1972, Dejean investigated the problem of determining, for each possible alphabet size, the threshold between exponents <math>e</math> for which there exists an infinite <math>e</math>-power-free word, and the exponents for which no such word exists. The problem was solved for two-symbol alphabets by the Thue–Morse sequence, and Dejean solved it as well for three-symbol alphabets.
She conjectured a precise formula for the threshold exponent for every larger alphabet size;{{r|dejean}} this formula is Dejean's conjecture, now a theorem.{{r|rs}}

==Statement==
Let <math>k</math> be the number of symbols in an alphabet.
For every <math>k</math>, define <math>\operatorname{RT}(k)</math>, the ''repeat threshold'', to be the [[infimum]] of exponents <math>e</math> such that there exists an infinite <math>e</math>-power-free word on a <math>k</math>-symbol alphabet. Thus, for instance, the Thue–Morse sequence shows that <math>\operatorname{RT}(2)=2</math>, and an argument based on the [[Lovász local lemma]] can be used to show that <math>\operatorname{RT}(k)</math> is finite for all <math>k</math>.{{r|rs}}

Then Dejean's conjecture is that the repeat threshold can be calculated by the simple formula{{r|rs|dejean}}
:<math>\operatorname{RT}(k)=\frac{k}{k-1}</math>
except in two exceptional cases:
:<math>\operatorname{RT}(3)=\frac{7}{4}</math>
and
:<math>\operatorname{RT}(4)=\frac{7}{5}.</math>

==Progress and proof==
Dejean herself proved the conjecture for <math>k=3</math>.{{r|dejean}}
The case <math>k=4</math> was proven by Jean-Jacques Pansiot in 1984.{{r|pansiot}}
The next progress was by Moulin Ollagnier in 1992, who proved the conjecture for all alphabet sizes up to <math>k\le 11</math>.{{r|mo}}
This analysis was extended up to <math>k\le 14</math> in 2007 by Mohammad-Noori and Currie.{{r|mc}}

In the other direction, also in 2007, Arturo Carpi showed the conjecture to be true for large alphabets, with <math>k\ge 33</math>.{{r|carpi}} This reduced the problem to a finite number of remaining cases, which were solved in 2009 and published in 2011 by Currie and Rampersad{{r|cr}} and independently by Rao.{{r|rao}}

==Dejean words==
An infinite string that meets Dejean's formula (having no repetitions of exponent above the repetition threshold) is called a '''Dejean word'''.
Thus, for instance, the Thue–Morse sequence is a Dejean word.
